paras.text: Bar Exam and Legal Foundations, Audio Lecture
This is the last chapter, and it does something different from the other nine.

Everything else was Michigan insurance law as it gets litigated. This one steps back a level. First, the mechanics of becoming a Michigan lawyer, straight from the Board of Law Examiners' rules. Second, the first year doctrines sitting underneath everything you already know.

That second half is the part that will surprise you. You have spent nine chapters learning insurance rules, and most of them turn out to be ordinary contract law wearing an insurance costume. When you see the doctrine underneath, the insurance rule stops being something to memorize and starts being something that follows.
Fifteen ideas. After most of them, a question and then silence. Answer out loud.
Idea one. Rule one, and a requirement that is not what everyone thinks.

Rule one sets three baseline requirements. Be eighteen or older. Possess good moral character. And, the one worth memorizing precisely, have completed, before entering law school, at least sixty semester hours or ninety quarter hours toward an undergraduate degree.
Now notice what it does not say. It does not require a finished bachelor's degree.

The four year degree almost every applicant has comes from the law school's own admission standard, not from this rule. So if a question claims Michigan itself requires a bachelor's degree before law school, that describes common practice, not the rule's text.
Sixty semester hours or ninety quarter hours. Those are the same amount of school counted two ways.
Idea two. Rule two, subsection B, where the degree pressure actually comes from.
Before sitting the exam you need a J D from a reputable and qualified law school.
A school approved by the American Bar Association is automatically reputable and qualified, with no petition needed.

Any other school can ask the Board to approve it. That is a discretionary call weighing relevant legal education and experience. So hear both halves: it is not a flat ban on non A B A degrees, and it is not a guarantee either.

And rule five, which lets a licensed out of state attorney skip the exam, does not dodge this. It expressly requires qualification under rules one and two B. There is no back door around the school requirement.
Idea three. Deadlines, character, and the M P R E.
Filing deadlines come in pairs, one per exam.
November first for the February exam, late until December fifteenth. March first for the July exam, late until May fifteenth.

Every applicant goes through a character and fitness investigation run by the State Bar's committee, and must disclose any criminal conviction carrying a possible penalty of incarceration that has not been reversed or vacated. Read that carefully. It is keyed to the possible penalty, not to whether anyone actually went to jail.

Every applicant must also pass the Multistate Professional Responsibility Exam, the M P R E, at the score the Board sets. That score is eighty five, and Michigan puts no time limit on when you took it.
Eighty five, and no expiration. Hold that, because in one minute you will meet a different number that does expire.
Idea four. The exam itself, and the number to memorize.
Rule three defines it as the Uniform Bar Exam, with three pieces.
The Multistate Bar Exam, the multiple choice portion. The Multistate Essay Exam, six essays. And two Multistate Performance Test items.
Who grades what: the National Conference of Bar Examiners grades the multiple choice portion, and the Michigan Board grades the essays and the performance test.
The weighting to know cold: multiple choice fifty percent, essays thirty percent, performance test twenty percent, on a four hundred point scale.
Fifty, thirty, twenty. They add to one hundred, which is how you check yourself.
The essay portion is six questions, thirty minutes each.
And Michigan's passing score, the number to memorize, is two hundred sixty eight.
Question. Michigan's passing score, the M P R E score, and the three exam weights.
Two hundred sixty eight to pass, on a four hundred point scale. Eighty five on the M P R E. And fifty percent multiple choice, thirty percent essays, twenty percent performance test.
Idea five. Portability, and the four part transfer test.
Three more mechanics, and they interlock.
To keep your score portable to another U B E state, you have to sit every component in one administration. And a passing score is good for three years.
Michigan also requires the Michigan Law Component, a course on state specific topics, before admission by any route. Any route means any route, including admission without examination.
Transferring a score in requires four things, all four.

It must meet or exceed two hundred sixty eight. It must have been earned within the three years immediately preceding the Michigan exam date you would otherwise have sat for. You must have taken the M P R E and hit Michigan's score. And you must complete the Michigan Law Component.
Miss one, even by a month on the three year clock, and the transfer fails. There is no partial credit and no rounding in your favor.
Idea six. Rule five, admission without examination, and its teeth.
This one sounds like a shortcut, and it is a narrow one.

You must qualify independently under rules one and two B. Be licensed and in good standing somewhere in the United States. Intend to practice or instruct full time in Michigan. And, after being licensed and for three of the five years preceding the application, have actively practiced law as a principal occupation, taught full time at a law school, or served on active duty as a judge advocate.
Three of the five years. Two years out of five does not clear that bar, though the Board can extend for good cause.
Fees. Four hundred dollars for the exam. Three hundred for reexamination. Eight hundred for admission without examination.

And a nice detail about the Board's own power. It can waive almost any requirement, but never the fees and never the administration of the exam. So the two things that can never be waived are money and actually taking the test.
Question. You have been licensed in Ohio for five years but only practiced two of them. Do you qualify for admission without examination?

No. Rule five requires actively practicing as a principal occupation, teaching full time, or serving as a judge advocate for three of the five years preceding the application. Two does not clear it, unless the Board extends for good cause.
Idea seven. NextGen, and a date to be careful about.
Michigan moves to the NextGen Uniform Bar Exam in July twenty twenty eight, the forty sixth jurisdiction to commit.

The last legacy exam here is February twenty twenty eight. And note where that date comes from, because sourcing matters: it comes from the legacy exam page's test dates, not from the NextGen press release.
NextGen runs about a day and a half, six hours on day one and three on day two. Compare that to the current twelve hours over two full days. It is a substantially shorter exam.
And the structure changes. It tests nine areas of doctrine together with seven foundational lawyering skills, rather than in separately labeled components.
One honest gap. Michigan's NextGen passing score is still to be announced. Do not guess at it, and do not assume it will be two hundred sixty eight.
Idea eight. The essay subjects already shrank.
This one is not a future change. The July twenty twenty six change already happened.

The National Conference of Bar Examiners now lists eight areas. Business associations. Civil procedure. Constitutional law. Contracts, including Article Two of the Uniform Commercial Code. Criminal law and procedure. Evidence. Real property. And torts.

The four that dropped out are conflict of laws, family law, trusts and estates, and secured transactions. With family law and trusts and estates moving to the performance test through February twenty twenty eight.
So they did not vanish entirely. Two of the four moved rather than left.
Idea nine. Where insurance actually lives on that list.
There is no subject called insurance law. But insurance concepts are baked into three tested subjects, and this is the bridge back to the last nine chapters.
Inside contracts: formation. Parol evidence, as its own named topic. Conditions, express and constructive. And remedies, including expectation interest and causation, certainty, and foreseeability.
Every one of those maps onto how a policy gets formed, read, and enforced. Because a policy is first a contract, and only second an insurance thing.
Inside torts, the negligence section names the duty question, the standard of care, proof of fault, causation, and defenses.
And inside evidence, a section called privileges and other policy exclusions names insurance coverage specifically.
Michigan's own version is M R E four eleven. Evidence that a person was or was not insured against liability is not admissible to prove whether the person acted negligently or otherwise wrongfully.

Now read the second sentence, because that is where the trap lives. The court may still admit that evidence for another purpose, such as proving a witness's bias or prejudice, or, if disputed, proving agency, ownership, or control.
The rule blocks the fault inference. It does not block every use of insurance evidence. Those are very different rules, and people state the first as if it were absolute.
Idea ten. Contract formation, where Michigan counts to five.
Here is a trap most study guides walk you straight into.
The national shorthand is four elements. Offer, acceptance, consideration, mutual assent.
Michigan courts recite five.

Hess versus Cannon Township, quoting Thomas versus Leja, gives them. One, parties competent to contract. Two, a proper subject matter. Three, a legal consideration. Four, mutuality of agreement, which is the meeting of the minds idea. Five, mutuality of obligation, meaning both sides are actually bound.
If a question asks for Michigan's formulation, give the five. Four is the national answer, not the Michigan one.

And the Michigan Supreme Court, in Titan Insurance Company versus Hyten, confirmed an insurance policy is treated like any other contract for these purposes, subject to the same construction principles as any other species of contract, unless a statute says otherwise.
That sentence is the whole reason this chapter belongs in an insurance track.
Idea eleven. Parol evidence, and who actually said the famous sentence.
The case is U A W dash G M Human Resource Center versus K S L Recreation Corporation, nineteen ninety eight.

The sentence everyone quotes is: parol evidence of contract negotiations, or of prior or contemporaneous agreements that contradict or vary the written contract, is not admissible to vary the terms of a contract which is clear and unambiguous.

But U A W dash G M did not write that sentence. It is quoting an earlier case, Schmude Oil Company versus Omar Operating Company. If you attribute it to U A W dash G M as its holding, you are one step off.

What U A W dash G M itself held is the merger clause half. When the parties include an integration clause, it is conclusive, and parol evidence cannot show the agreement is not integrated. Two exceptions only: fraud that invalidates the integration clause itself, or where the writing is obviously incomplete on its face. A merger clause, the court said, nullifies all antecedent agreements.
Picture how that lands in your world. An adjuster tells a homeowner over the phone that the whole roof is covered. But the signed appraisal agreement lists two slopes and carries a merger clause.
That phone call cannot override the writing, because the clause made reliance on anything outside the document unreasonable.
Idea twelve. Three fraud doctrines, and two citations people swap.
The same case sorts out three fraud doctrines that get mixed up constantly.
Actionable fraud is the affirmative lie.
Silent fraud, also called fraudulent concealment, is the failure to divulge a fact the defendant had a duty to disclose. Note the duty. Silence is only fraud when you were obligated to speak.
Innocent misrepresentation drops the knowledge requirement but adds privity. A trade: you no longer have to show they knew, but you do have to be in a direct contractual relationship.

Now get the citations right, because they are easy to swap. U A W dash G M cites McMullen versus Joldersma for silent fraud, and U S Fidelity and Guaranty versus Black for innocent misrepresentation. Not the reverse.
Question. Name the three fraud doctrines, what distinguishes each, and which case goes with which of the last two.

Actionable fraud, the affirmative lie. Silent fraud, failure to disclose where there was a duty, McMullen versus Joldersma. Innocent misrepresentation, no knowledge requirement but privity required, U S Fidelity and Guaranty versus Black.
Idea thirteen. Conditions precedent, and the proof of loss rule they explain.
This ties straight back to the deadlines you already learned.

Michigan's definition is intent based, not the Restatement phrasing. Harbor Park Market versus Gronda, quoting Mikonczyk: a condition precedent is a fact or event that the parties intend must take place before there is a right to performance. If it is not satisfied, there is no cause of action for failure to perform.

And the flip side matters enormously when the insurer is the one holding things up. A promisor who prevents the condition waives it, because there is an implied agreement that the promisor will place no obstacle in the way of the happening of such event.

Michigan courts apply that hard to a fire policy's sworn proof of loss requirement. The rule, restated across published Court of Appeals cases: failure to timely provide a sworn statement in proof of loss within the policy's explicit time requirement is an absolute bar to the insured's recovery.

Now note what does not save the insured. Prejudice. Dellar says the failure bars recovery without regard to whether the insurer was prejudiced. It does not matter that the carrier was not hurt by the delay.
What does save the insured is waiver or estoppel. And the two cases together draw the line cleanly.
In Dellar the insurer never sent the policy despite two timely demands, and the insured said she never got a proof of loss form. That was enough to put waiver and estoppel to a factfinder.
Compare Willett, where the insurer did send a letter stating the requirement, did enclose the blank form, and did warn of the consequence. There the estoppel argument went nowhere.
So the difference between those two cases is entirely about what the carrier sent. That is a genuinely useful thing to notice in a real file.

The same logic runs through Dupree versus Auto dash Owners, four ninety seven Michigan one. A policy paying only actual cash value until repair or replacement is completed left a claimant who never proved completed repair with actual cash value only, even after an appraisal award. The Court called the missing proof of actual loss a condition precedent, and M C L five hundred point two eight two six expressly permits that kind of clause.
Idea fourteen. Damages, and why a wrongly delayed claim rarely pays for the suffering.

Hadley versus Baxendale, as Michigan adopted it in Kewin versus Massachusetts Mutual Life: the damages recoverable for breach of contract are those that arise naturally from the breach, or those in the contemplation of the parties when the contract was made.

Applied to an ordinary contract, that caps damages at the contract's value as if performed. So a policyholder generally cannot recover for the emotional toll of a wrongly delayed claim, however real that toll is.

Kewin recognizes one narrow exception, from Stewart versus Rudner. Contracts concerned with life and death rather than trade and commerce, matters of mental concern and solicitude. The facts there were a doctor's broken promise to deliver a child by Caesarean section.
And Kewin declined to extend that exception to an ordinary disability policy. So the exception exists, and insurance is on the wrong side of it.

Kewin is also the source of the bad faith rule you met in chapter four: a bad faith breach of an insurance contract, standing alone, does not create an independent tort claim, absent a duty independent of and apart from the contractual undertaking.
Idea fifteen. Fraud's six elements, negligence's four, and the limitations numbers.
Fraud first, Titan versus Hyten again. The six element test for actionable fraud.
A material representation. That was false. Made knowingly or recklessly. With intent that the plaintiff act on it. Actual reliance. And resulting injury.
All six must be proven. Missing one is fatal.

The facts are a favorite trap. The insurer issued an auto policy after the applicant checked a box saying no driver in the household had a suspended license, when the license was in fact suspended, something the insurer could have checked against Secretary of State records.

The Court of Appeals said that because the fraud was easily discoverable, the insurer could not use it against an injured third party. The Supreme Court reversed, overruling the easily ascertainable rule.

Learn the broader sentence, because it is the real holding: none of Michigan's fraud doctrines requires the party asserting fraud to prove the fraud could not have been discovered through the exercise of reasonable diligence. There is no duty to investigate.
Negligence next, and it is the freshest doctrine here, rewritten by the Michigan Supreme Court in twenty twenty three.
The core elements, restated in Kandil-Elsayed versus F and E Oil, five twelve Michigan ninety five: every negligence action requires four essential elements. Duty, breach, causation, and harm.

What changed is where the open and obvious nature of a hazard fits. For over twenty years, under Lugo, an open and obvious danger defeated duty altogether, unless the plaintiff showed special aspects, meaning an effectively unavoidable hazard or a substantial risk of death or severe injury.
Kandil-Elsayed threw that out. Open and obvious is now folded into breach and Michigan's comparative fault statutes, decided by the jury.

The division that survives is worth saying cleanly. Whether a duty exists remains a question of law for the court. Whether it was breached is a question of fact for the jury, open and obvious included.
Now statutes of limitation, quickly.
M C L six hundred point five eight zero five governs torts. Three years after death or injury for damage to a person or property is the default, with named exceptions on top.

Two years for assault, battery, or false imprisonment, but five years where the assault was by a spouse, former spouse, household member, or dating partner. Ten years for criminal sexual conduct. Two years for malicious prosecution and for malpractice. One year for libel or slander. Three years for products liability.
M C L six hundred point five eight zero seven governs contracts, and its residual rule, subsection nine, covering an ordinary breach not described elsewhere in the section, sets six years.

Now burn this trap in, because it is the one that ties this chapter to chapter three. That six year period does not control a Standard Fire Policy suit. The fire policy has its own one year suit limitation, tolled from notice to formal denial, and that specific insurance code deadline controls.
If a question describes a fire policy dispute and offers six years, that is the wrong statute.
Last, evidence, and keep two separate orders straight, because one is cosmetic and one is not.

First, administrative file twenty twenty one dash ten restyled the whole body of evidence rules effective January first, twenty twenty four, to stay as consistent as possible with the twenty eleven restyling of the federal rules. That was formatting, not substance, and the order says so.

Second, administrative file twenty twenty two dash thirty amended Rule seven oh two and Rule eight oh four effective May first, twenty twenty four. That one is substantive. The party offering an expert must now show it is more likely than not that the admission requirements are satisfied, and it is the expert's opinion that must reflect a reliable application of principles and methods to the facts.

Federal Rule of Evidence seven oh two, amended effective December first, twenty twenty three, now reads the same way. But the Michigan order never says it was copying it. So state it carefully: the texts match. That is the claim you can defend, and it is different from claiming Michigan copied the federal rule.
One last thing, and it is not testable, so keep it off the flashcards.

Jacob's own plan runs through an undergraduate degree satisfying the sixty credit floor, an online A B A approved law degree, and the Michigan bar around twenty thirty one. That is a personal plan, not a Board rule. Do not let it sit in your memory next to the actual requirements as though it had the same status.

Everything else here, the two hundred sixty eight score, the eighty five M P R E, the three year windows, the five element Michigan contract test, the six element fraud test, the four element negligence test, and the limitations numbers, those are the rules.
Time for the rapid fire recap. Fast, as a self check.

Rule one, eighteen or older, good moral character, sixty semester hours or ninety quarter hours before law school, no bachelor's degree required by the rule. Rule two B, a J D from a reputable and qualified school, A B A approved is automatic. Filing November first for February, March first for July, late until December fifteenth and May fifteenth. M P R E eighty five, no time limit. Uniform Bar Exam, multiple choice fifty percent, essays thirty percent, performance test twenty percent, four hundred point scale, six essays at thirty minutes each, passing score two hundred sixty eight, portable for three years. Michigan Law Component required by any route. Rule five, three of the five preceding years in practice, teaching, or as a judge advocate. Fees four hundred, three hundred, eight hundred, never waivable. NextGen July twenty twenty eight, last legacy exam February twenty twenty eight, passing score not yet announced. Eight essay subjects since July twenty twenty six. M R E four eleven blocks the fault inference only. Michigan contract formation, five elements. Merger clause is conclusive under U A W dash G M. Silent fraud is McMullen versus Joldersma, innocent misrepresentation is U S Fidelity and Guaranty versus Black. Sworn proof of loss is an absolute bar regardless of prejudice, defeated only by waiver or estoppel. Hadley damages, arising naturally or in contemplation, no emotional distress for an ordinary policy. Fraud, six elements, and no duty to investigate after Titan versus Hyten. Negligence, four elements, and open and obvious now goes to breach after Kandil-Elsayed. Torts three years default under six hundred point five eight zero five, contracts six years under five eight zero seven, and neither one controls a fire policy suit.
Know them cold. And if any of the questions I asked gave you trouble, that is exactly where to drill.
